title: West Virginia's $12,000 Bet Pays Off: Digital Nomads Are Putting Down Roots
summary: When Ashley Eklin was diagnosed with multiple sclerosis in 2022, she decided to take a "huge leap of faith." She quit her life in Chicago, bought a house sight unseen in Inwood, West Virginia — population 3,400 — and moved there with her two dogs. The catalyst? A program called Ascend West Virginia that offered her $12,000 to relocate. "I literally had never been to West Virginia. I hadn't even visited, and I bought a house," Eklin says. Three years later, she's kayaking, hiking, and learning astrophotography under dark, unpolluted skies. Ascend West Virginia launched in 2021, the 50th anniversary of John Denver's "Take Me Home, Country Roads." It was the brainchild of Brad D. Smith, former Intuit CEO and a West Virginia native, who funded it with $25 million from his Wing 2 Wing Foundation. The goal: reverse the state's staggering population decline. West Virginia is the only U.S. state with fewer residents than in 1950, and it ranks among the highest in poverty. But it boasts a low cost of living and world-class outdoor recreation — rugged mountains, whitewater rivers, dense forests. "What we recognized is that West Virginia has some of the highest density and highest caliber of outdoor recreation in the entire country," says Danny Twilley of West Virginia University, who helped design the program. Unlike many relocation incentives that use taxpayer money, Ascend West Virginia is privately funded. It's part of a wave of similar programs that emerged during the pandemic, when remote work untethered millions of Americans from offices. The idea is simple: attract remote workers with cash, and they'll boost the local economy. So far, it's working. The program has spawned spinoffs: First Ascent to retain college grads, Teachers Ascend to recruit educators, and Ascend Heroes for veterans. For Abby Snyder and Colin Scott, a couple who had been living as digital nomads in Portugal, the decision to move to Lewisburg was about more than money. "We need to be part of this fight for our democracy and fight for environmentalism and art and people," Snyder says. They're now putting down roots in Appalachia. The program's success suggests that for many, the promise of community and natural beauty — plus a financial nudge — is enough to call West Virginia home.
why_it_matters: This story shows how a single creative policy, backed by private money, can try to solve a decades-long problem. For young people, it illustrates that where we live is increasingly a choice tied to lifestyle, not just a nearby office — and that struggling regions can reinvent themselves when remote work opens the door.

background_read: Remote work became widespread during the COVID-19 pandemic, allowing millions of employees to work from anywhere with an internet connection. This gave rise to 'digital nomads' — people who live in different places while working online.

West Virginia is part of Appalachia, a mountainous region known for coal mining history, poverty, and cultural richness. The state's population peaked in 1950 and has declined ever since, making it an unusual case in a growing nation.

John Denver's 'Take Me Home, Country Roads' (1971) famously mentions West Virginia’s natural beauty and became an unofficial state anthem. The song's 50th anniversary gave the Ascend program a symbolic launch date.
Brad D. Smith, a West Virginia native, was the CEO of Intuit (the company behind TurboTax and QuickBooks) before founding the Wing 2 Wing Foundation, which privately funds the relocation initiative.

perspectives.description: Newcomers like Ashley Eklin gain a healthier, more affordable lifestyle surrounded by nature, while long-time locals see fresh energy and spending in towns that had been shrinking. The program turns a state’s weakness (low population) into a selling point.

Some may worry that a few thousand remote workers can't fix deep-rooted poverty, and that private-funded programs might not last if the donor’s interest fades. Others argue that attracting outsiders could drive up housing costs for existing residents who did not receive a $12,000 check.

Relocation incentives are not new — towns and states have tried them for decades with mixed results. Ascend West Virginia’s twist is using remote work and outdoor branding to target a national talent pool, raising the question of whether place-based cash grants can truly reverse long-term economic decline.

If the program keeps showing results, more regions may adopt similar private incentive models. The real test will be whether newcomers stay for a decade, start businesses, and raise families, or drift away when the next trendy spot offers a bigger check. West Virginia’s experiment could rewrite how struggling communities compete in the remote-work era.
